Hello, I'm so glad you're here today. My name is [Your Name], and I'm a clinician specializing in postpartum mental health. I want to start by acknowledging the significant journey you've been on, becoming a new mother. This can be a life-changing experience, filled with a wide range of emotions. As part of our care for you during this period, we use a tool called the EPDS to help understand how you're feeling and to provide the best support possible.

The EPDS is designed to screen for depressive and anxiety symptoms, which can sometimes arise during the postpartum period. It's a valuable tool that helps us understand your emotional well-being and ensure that you receive any necessary support. Please know that everything discussed here is confidential and held in a safe, supportive space. We're here to listen and help in any way we can.

This assessment will involve going through 10 questions that will help us understand your feelings and experiences over the past week. These questions are designed to be straightforward and will give us a clearer picture of how you're doing. Don't worry about answering "right" or "wrong"; we just want to hear your honest thoughts and feelings.

Let's get started. The first question is about how you've been feeling over the past week. Have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things as easily as you used to?

I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I'd say that's still pretty much the case for me. I mean, being a new mom can be really overwhelming at times, but I've been able to find the humor in things and laugh with my family and friends. Like, the other day, my baby spit up all over me, and at first, I was frustrated, but then I just couldn't help but laugh at the mess. It's moments like those that remind me to not take things too seriously. So, yeah, I'd say I'm still able to laugh and see the funny side of things, which is a good feeling.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I've still been looking forward to things, like spending time with my baby, taking walks with my family, and catching up with friends. Sometimes, I get a bit tired from caring for the baby, but when I have something to look forward to, it gives me the energy to keep going. Like, my husband and I planned a little outing with the baby to the park last weekend, and I was really excited about it. It was nice to get out of the house and enjoy the fresh air together. I've also been enjoying those small moments, like bath time with the baby or reading a book together. Those things bring me joy and make me feel happy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I wouldn't say that's been a big issue for me. I mean, I'm sure every new mom makes mistakes or worries that they're not doing things perfectly, but I haven't been too hard on myself. If something doesn't go as planned, I try to just roll with it and figure out a solution. Like, the other day, I forgot to pack an extra diaper in the baby's bag, and we had a bit of a mess on our hands. But instead of beating myself up over it, I just laughed and said, "Well, that was a rookie mistake!" My husband was really supportive, and we just dealt with it together. I try not to dwell on things that don't go right, and I remind myself that I'm doing the best I can as a new mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I'd say I've had a few moments where I've felt a bit worried, but it's usually about the baby's health or something specific that's going on with them. Like, if they're not feeding well or if they have a fever, I get a little anxious. But it's not like I'm lying awake at night worrying about nothing in particular. I think it's just normal new mom worries, you know? I mean, you want everything to be perfect for your baby, and sometimes that can be a bit overwhelming. But overall, I wouldn't say I've been feeling anxious or worried for no good reason. It's usually something specific that's triggering it, and once I address that issue or talk to my husband or doctor about it, I feel better.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

No, I don't think so. I mean, I've had some overwhelming moments as a new mom, but I wouldn't say I've felt scared or panicky for no reason. Like I mentioned earlier, if something's going on with the baby, I might get a little worried, but it's not like I'm feeling scared or panicky out of the blue. I've been able to manage my emotions and calm myself down when I start to feel overwhelmed. My husband has been really supportive, and just talking to him or taking a few deep breaths usually helps me feel better. I don't think I've had any moments where I've felt suddenly scared or panicky without a reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah. I mean, being a new mom can be really exhausting, and some days it feels like everything is piling up. But it's not like I'm feeling completely overwhelmed all the time. I'd say it's more like... occasional moments where I feel like, "Okay, I don't know how I'm going to get everything done today." But then I take a step back, prioritize what needs to be done, and ask for help if I need it. My husband is really great about pitching in and supporting me, so that helps a lot. And, you know, some days are just better than others. But overall, I'd say I'm managing okay. I'm not feeling like things are getting on top of me all the time, just occasionally when I'm feeling really tired or stressed.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, that's not really been an issue for me. I mean, I've had some tired nights, of course, because the baby doesn't always sleep through the night, but when I do get to sleep, I've been sleeping pretty well. I wouldn't say I've been unhappy to the point where it's affecting my sleep. Like I said, some days are tougher than others, but overall, I've been feeling pretty stable and able to manage my emotions. I've been trying to take care of myself, too, and get some rest when I can, even if it's just a nap during the day. So, sleep hasn't really been a problem for me, thankfully.
I have felt sad or miserable

Not really. I mean, I've had some tough moments as a new mom, but I wouldn't say I've felt sad or miserable. I've been feeling a little fatigued at times, just because taking care of a newborn can be exhausting, but that's about it. I've been enjoying spending time with my baby and watching them grow, and that's been really rewarding for me. I've also been feeling supported by my husband and family, which has made a big difference. I don't feel like I've been feeling sad or miserable, just... tired, sometimes. But that's to be expected, right.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I mean, I've had a few tears here and there, but it's not like I've been crying all the time or feeling overwhelmingly unhappy. I think I've just had a few emotional moments, you know, when I'm feeling tired or overwhelmed, but they've been pretty rare. I'd say I've cried maybe once or twice since the baby was born, and it was just because I was feeling a bit overwhelmed, but it wasn't like I was feeling deeply sad or unhappy. It was more just a release of emotions, you know? And after I cried, I felt a bit better, and I was able to move on. So, no, I wouldn't say I've been crying a lot or feeling really unhappy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

No. I can honestly say that's not something I've ever thought about. I mean, I've had some tough moments as a new mom, but I've never felt like I wanted to harm myself. I've been feeling a little overwhelmed at times, but I've always been able to talk to my husband or family about it and get the support I need. I've never felt like I was in a place where I would consider harming myself. That's just not something that's ever crossed my mind, and I feel really fortunate to be able to say that. I think it's really important for new moms to talk about their feelings and get support, and I feel like I've been doing that, so... no, that's not something I've ever thought about.

As a new mother, you've shared your experiences and emotions with me, and I want to acknowledge the challenges and joys that come with this significant life change. It's clear that you're doing your best to navigate the ups and downs of caring for your newborn, and that's something to be proud of. I'm here to support you and provide guidance as you continue on this journey.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 4: **Postpartum Depression Screening Summary**

The patient, a new mother, presented with overall positive emotional and behavioral responses, indicating a relatively stable mood and ability to cope with the challenges of caring for a newborn. Key observations include:

* The patient reports being able to laugh, find humor, and look forward to activities, suggesting preserved pleasure and enjoyment.
* She expresses some anxiety and worry, primarily related to the baby's health, but these concerns appear situation-specific and manageable.
* The patient denies persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, and crying spells, which are common indicators of postpartum depression.
* She reports some difficulty with sleep, attributed to the baby's nighttime needs, but this does not appear to be linked to mood disturbances.
* The patient expresses feelings of being overwhelmed at times, but these emotions are intermittent and managed with support from her husband and self-care strategies.
* There is no indication of worthlessness, guilt, or self-harm/suicidal thoughts, which are critical risk factors for postpartum depression.

**Screening Significance:**

* The patient's ability to experience pleasure, laugh, and look forward to activities suggests a low risk for postpartum depression.
* Situation-specific anxiety and worry related to the baby's health are common in new mothers and do not necessarily indicate a pathological condition.
* The absence of persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, and crying spells reduces the likelihood of postpartum depression.
* The patient's support system, self-care strategies, and ability to manage overwhelming emotions contribute to a lower risk profile.

**Risk Factors:**

* None of the critical risk factors for postpartum depression, such as persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, crying spells, or self-harm/suicidal thoughts, were identified in this screening.
* The patient's anxiety and worry, although situation-specific, should be monitored to ensure they do not escalate or become more pervasive.

**Screening Observation Summary:**

This postpartum depression screening suggests a low risk for postpartum depression or anxiety disorders. The patient's emotional and behavioral responses indicate a relatively stable mood, ability to cope with challenges, and a supportive environment. Continued monitoring and support are recommended to ensure the patient's emotional well-being, particularly during the postpartum period.
